sections.body:
A **gender role** is a rule that a culture attaches to a category of people: what a man is expected to do, what a woman is expected to do. The role is not a description of anybody. It is a description of what people expect, what they watch for, and what they say when the expectation is not met. The word *expected* does most of the work here: a role says what follows if you do a certain thing, and it says nothing about what you are.

Three things travel together in this subject, and they are easy to mix up. A **stereotype** is a claim about what a person is: *men are bad with feelings*, *women cannot lead a team*. A role is a claim about what a person should do. A **gender identity** is the sense a person has of their own gender, and it belongs to that person. A **gender expression** is how that identity is shown in the world: the clothes, the voice, the gesture, the way a person stands in a room. A role can be assigned to somebody whose identity does not match it, and it is still the role that was assigned.

The three are treated in different ways, which is why the difference is worth keeping. A stereotype is usually checked against the person in front of you, and it loses. A role is enforced: it is checked before you speak, before you are hired, before you are introduced to somebody. An identity is not checked at all. It is not a claim that anybody else gets to grade.

One limit belongs at the start. A role is a description of a pattern, not a verdict on a person, and the pattern is not the same in every family, workplace or country. The same rule can be strict in one house and loose in the next. This article describes the mechanism and gives you the words for it. It does not tell you what to do with your own life.
examples: A role is a rule about what to do; a stereotype is a claim about what somebody is.
The gender role was handed to her at school, and she never agreed to it.
His gender expression changed with the job, and the new fit was easier.
Gender identity is hers to say, and nobody else gets a vote.
sections.heading: A gender role is a rule about what to do

terms.example: The gender role said the man pays, and the rule was never written down.
terms.gloss: A rule about what a category of people is expected to do.

terms.example: Her gender identity was hers to say, and nobody in the room had a vote on it.
terms.gloss: The sense a person has of their own gender.

terms.example: His gender expression changed when he started a new job, and the fit got easier.
terms.gloss: How a person presents their gender through clothes, voice, gesture and behaviour.

terms.example: That was a stereotype, not an observation: nobody in the room had looked at the man in front of them.
terms.gloss: A belief about a group that is applied to a person without looking at that person.

sections.body:
Nobody is handed a role in a speech. A role arrives in small pieces, from the people around you, over years. The family gives the first version: the child who is given the toy kitchen and the child who is given the tool set learns the division before anybody explains it. School adds what the group rewards and what it punishes. Work adds what is given to the person who is expected to do a job, and what is quietly taken away when they do not. Media and peers repeat the whole thing, in stories and in jokes, and a joke is a cheap way to teach a rule nobody wants to admit is a rule.

The result is a rule that everybody can state and nobody chose. When somebody breaks it, the cost is usually not a rule that says *this is forbidden*. The cost is a set of small penalties: a joke that lands badly, a reputation that is hard to repair, a task that is given to somebody else instead, a partner who says *you are being difficult*. A penalty does not have to be large to work. It only has to be enough.

The cost falls hardest on the person who breaks the rule, because the rule is held in two places at once: in the expectation of the group, and in the acceptance of the person inside the group. The person who follows it pays nothing for following it. The person who does not pays for the whole arrangement, including the part of it they were keeping alive. This is why the pressure to conform is strongest exactly where the cost is invisible, and why the person who gives something up to change the arrangement is often described as the one who caused the problem.

Two words help here. A **double bind** is a situation in which a person is given two rules that cannot both be satisfied: be the one who decides and be the one who notices that everybody is exhausted; be the one who earns and be the one who is always available. The person inside a bind cannot solve it by trying harder, because the second rule cancels the first. And **hegemonic masculinity** describes the pattern in which one form of manliness becomes the standard everybody is measured against: decisive, unemotional, financially reliable. The other forms of manliness are then treated as lesser versions of it. Researchers disagree about how much of that pattern comes from culture and how much from other causes, and the argument is open; but the pattern and its penalties are visible to anybody who has watched a team or a family.
examples: The role was taught in small pieces, and nobody asked to learn it.
The penalty was small every time, and small was enough.
Be the one who decides and be the one who notices everybody is tired: that is a double bind.
One form of manliness became the standard, and the others were measured against it.
sections.heading: How a role is assigned, and what it costs to break one

terms.example: A double bind: be the one who decides, and be the one who notices that everybody is exhausted.
terms.gloss: A situation in which a person is given two rules that cannot both be satisfied.

terms.example: Hegemonic masculinity sets the picture of the man who never complains, and the man who does is treated as a smaller version of it.
terms.gloss: The pattern in which one form of manliness becomes the standard everybody is measured against.

sections.body:
Three words carry most of the work in this subject, and they are easy to confuse because they sound like descriptions of the same thing.

A **prescriptive norm** is a rule about what people should do: *a man should pay for the meal*, *a woman should speak up in a meeting*, *the father stays at home with the baby*. A **descriptive norm** is what the people around you actually do, whether or not it is written anywhere: the same office where everybody stays for the handover, the same family where one person books every appointment. The first says what is expected, the second says what is usual. They can point in opposite directions, and where they do the descriptive norm is usually the stronger force, because it is the one with a daily example.

A **role conflict** is the strain that appears when one person is expected to be two things at once and the two pull in different directions: the parent who is also the shift worker, the colleague who is also the mentor, the partner who is also the carer. A role conflict is not evidence that somebody is doing the job badly. It is evidence that two roles have been handed to one person without a conversation about the time they need.

The three words work together. A descriptive norm tells you what is usual in the room. A prescriptive norm tells you what is expected of you there. A role conflict is what you get when your own part does not fit both of them at once.
examples: It is a prescriptive norm: it says what should happen, not what does happen.
The descriptive norm here is that the team stays after the handover, and the expectation follows the team.
A role conflict is not a failure of effort; two roles were given to one week.
The usual and the expected can point in different directions, and the usual usually wins.
sections.heading: The words that describe the machinery

terms.example: It is a prescriptive norm: the expectation, not a description of what happens.
terms.gloss: A rule about what people should do.

terms.example: The descriptive norm here is that the whole team stays for the handover, and the expectation follows the team.
terms.gloss: What the people around you actually do, whether or not it is written down.

terms.example: The role conflict was not a failure of effort; two jobs had been given to one week.
terms.gloss: The strain that appears when one person is expected to be two things at once and the two pull in different directions.

sections.body:
A relationship is one of the places where roles are most complete, because a relationship has its own jobs: money, time, planning, remembering, repair. One common arrangement gives one partner the pursuit, the proposal and the financial weight, and the other partner the calendar, the family contact and the running of the household. In some couples the arrangement is the reverse, in some it is shared, and in some it changes over the years. What is worth naming is that the arrangement is a set of expectations, and each partner tends to read the other's expectations as what the other one wants.

Four words describe the work inside that arrangement. **Care work** is the work of keeping other people fed, rested, healthy and connected: the appointments, the medication, the school run, the ageing parent. **Household labour** is the work of the house itself: cleaning, shopping, cooking, laundry, bills and repairs. The two overlap, and many people use one word for both. **Emotional labour** is the effort of managing your own feelings and other people's feelings so that the relationship keeps running: the tone you set, the mood you repair, the face you keep when you would rather not. It is a job, and in every couple somebody is doing it, usually without a title.

The **breadwinner** is the member of a couple who is expected to be the main earner, and the word carries the whole arrangement with it: the money, the standing, the right to have a say in what the money buys, and the duty to provide. When the household income depends on one person's job, that person's risk becomes the family's risk, and the other member is left to manage what happens if the job goes. Some couples keep that role, some refuse the label, and many share the earning.

Here is the part that surprises people. Both partners can be inside an arrangement and be unhappy inside it. The person who earns can feel that the earning is the whole price; the person who does the care work can feel that the care work is invisible, and that being asked is not the same as being thanked. A common source of the feeling is that the two partners are solving different problems: one is trying to feel safe, the other is trying to feel appreciated. And an arrangement nobody reviews keeps running after the people in it have changed. The asymmetry is not a sign that one partner is failing. It is a set of jobs that nobody wrote down and nobody checks.
examples: Care work is the appointments and the calls, and it is still work.
Emotional labour is the tone you set and the mood you repair, and it never appears on a rota.
The breadwinner carried the risk, and the risk became the family's.
The arrangement is a set of expectations, and nobody checks it unless somebody says so.

sections.body:
The table is a reading instrument, not a list of laws. Each row names a role that many couples, families and workplaces still carry, the expectation that comes with it, the people who usually enforce it, and the cost that lands on the person who does not follow it.

Two columns carry most of the weight. **Who enforces it** tells you where the pressure comes from, because a rule enforced by the people you love costs more than a rule enforced by strangers. **What happens when it is broken** tells you the currency of the penalty: status, money, time, silence, or a name you are given.

Use the table to name a pattern, never to win an argument. A row is a sentence you can start a conversation with — *this looks like the rule where one person keeps the calendar* — and the rest of the conversation belongs to the people inside it.
examples: This looks like the rule where one person keeps the calendar.
The enforcement tells you the price: a joke, a reputation, a task that moves.
Name the pattern first; the conversation about the arrangement comes after.
sections.heading: The expectation, the people who enforce it, and the cost of breaking it

headers: What happens when it is broken
rows: The one who pursues
You make the first move, you ask, you propose.
Friends, family and colleagues who hear about it.
The other person waits, the question gets older, and the silence is read as a no.
The one who pays
You cover the costs, or you carry the larger share of them.
The family, the guests, the bank, the workplace that pays.
The partner who expected to pay loses standing in front of others and has to explain the change.
The one who plans
You arrange the trip, the meal, the appointments, the calendar.
The other partner, who has to live inside the plan.
The planning stops, and the other partner is left holding the whole thing, or the arrangement is renegotiated.
The one who keeps the mood
You notice the mood, you repair the conflict, you keep the tone.
Everybody in the house, because everybody feels it.
The temperature drops, the house runs on silence, and the person who left the job is called the difficult one.
The one who is strong
You do not complain, you do not show weakness, you absorb the risk.
Peers, the workplace, and the family that reads it as proof.
The person who says they are tired is called weak, and the rule is confirmed by the answer.
The one who adapts
You change your plans and your schedule when somebody else needs you.
The person whose needs change.
The person who adapts is never asked again, because adapting always works and asking never does.

sections.body:
Six steps. They take one conversation, and they work with a partner, with a family member and with a team. The point of them is timing: a division agreed in a calm week survives a bad week, and a division left open is settled by whoever is most tired when the bad week arrives.

The first two steps put the rule on the table without an accusation, because a rule has to be visible before it can be changed. The third and fourth give each side a version of the arrangement that it can actually live with. The last two make the agreement survive the next busy week, which is when every unwritten arrangement is tested.

If the talk never happens, nothing changes. The old division keeps running, and the only decisions left are the small ones taken in a hurry: who goes to the appointment, who answers the message, who stays late. **Role negotiation** is what turns those small decisions into a choice you both made.
examples: In this house I keep the calendar, and I would like to look at that.
Who decided this, and when?
Let us write the division down before the busy week starts.
sections.heading: How to negotiate a role before a crisis decides it
steps: Name the rule in plain words, without an accusation: *in this house I keep the calendar and the appointments, and I would like to look at that.*
Ask where the rule came from: *who decided this, and when?* Sometimes the answer is a rule carried in from another household, and saying it out loud is enough to change it.
Say what your version of it is, in specifics: not *you never do anything*, but *I will take the hospital appointments and the school if you take the invoices and the car*.
Say what each side gets. A division that costs one partner something needs the other side to name the gain, so the arrangement does not become a silent sacrifice.
Write the division down before the busy week, and put it where both of you can see it. An agreement that lives only in the memory of the conversation is settled again by the first crisis.
Review it at a fixed time, and change it when it stops working. A role negotiation is not one event; it is a short routine.

terms.example: Role negotiation is not a quarrel about who is right; it is a decision about who does what.
terms.gloss: The talk in which two people change or confirm the roles they play together.

sections.body:
This article describes patterns, not laws. A role is not the same in every culture, and inside one culture it changes with class, with age and with the generation a person grows up in. A household that splits the work in a way nobody around them approves of is not breaking a rule; it is making a different arrangement. The patterns here are common enough to be worth recognising, and recognising one is not the same as obeying it.

Nobody is a prisoner of a role. A role is an expectation held by other people, and an expectation can be questioned, negotiated, accepted or refused — at the price that a refusal sometimes has to be paid. People also move between roles over a lifetime: the same person may be expected to be the strong one at work and the soft one at home, and both expectations can be wrong for that person.

And the reader may be anywhere on the spectrum of roles. A person may want to keep the traditional division, want to share it, or want something else again, and none of those positions is the subject of this article. The subject is the machinery: the vocabulary, the way a rule is assigned and enforced, the cost of breaking it, and the steps that put the division on the table before a crisis decides it.
examples: This describes a pattern, not a law, and the pattern is not the same everywhere.
A role is an expectation held by other people, and an expectation can be negotiated.
Recognising a rule is not the same as obeying it.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
Use these at the moment the rule shows itself. The first group is for a partner, the second for work, the third for a family member. Each sentence names the pattern first and the request second, because a pattern that is named can be discussed, while a request that arrives without a name is usually answered as an accusation.

Keep the voice flat. The point is not to win the exchange; it is to put the arrangement on the table in words that both people can hear without having to defend themselves.
examples: In this house I keep the calendar, and I would like to look at that.
We agreed to this division two years ago, and it does not fit us any more.
I can pay for it, but I cannot also plan it. Can we split those two?
You do the emotional work in this family, and nobody asks you to.
This is the third time I am the one who does the handover. Let us put the rotation in writing.
I am used to being the person who stays late for the difficult part, and I am saying no this time.
The team expects one person to fix the mood, and that person is always the same. Let us put the name on the rota.
I will take the client and you take the report. That is the arrangement I can work with.
In our family the son is the one who drives the grandmother to the clinic, and that is how it has always been.
You say it is my job because you are used to it, not because we agreed it.
We can keep the old arrangement if you want it, and I will say what it costs me.
Let us decide the division when things are calm, not in the week when everything happens at once.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

item.summary: A gender role is a rule about what a category of people is expected to do. After reading this you can tell a role from a stereotype, name who enforces the rule around you, see how the cost of breaking it falls on one person, and negotiate a division of work at home or at work before the next crisis decides it for you.
item.title: Gender Roles and Social Expectations
